title: Pine pencil tray
subtitle: Seasoned wood: a desk pencil and pen tray with dividers, cut and nailed from pine
excerpt: A rectangular pine tray with one divider, sized to hold pencils and pens on a desk. The box is cut from a standard pine board with a tenon saw and assembled with panel pins and wood glue. A beginner's box project that teaches accurate layout and squaring before gluing.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the box joint and pin-nail method; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the pine tray construction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fine, headless nail used for thin wood assembly. The pin is driven flush with the surface and does not require countersinking.
The simplest wood joint: two square-cut ends butted together and held with nails or glue. Used here for all the tray corners.

content.text: A pine pencil tray is a flat-base rectangular box with straight sides and one internal divider. The finished tray sits on a desk and holds long and short writing tools in two separate sections. It is a first box project, all joints are simple
butt joints
glued and pinned with
panel pins

, the measurements are straightforward, and the result is both useful and satisfying to make. The key skills are accurate measurement, square cutting with the tenon saw, and squaring the assembly before the glue sets.
What you need
Wood

One softwood pine board, PAR (planed all round), 100 cm long, 10 cm wide, 8 mm thick. From this board you cut: one base (32 cm × 10 cm), two long sides (32 cm × 4 cm), two short sides (10 cm × 4 cm), one divider (10 cm × 4 cm). Pine is the right choice for a first box: it cuts and sands easily and is cheap enough to not matter if the first attempt is imperfect.
Tools
Tenon saw for all straight cuts.
Combination square for marking and checking.
Marking gauge for consistent thickness marks.
Sandpaper 120 and 240 grit.
Panel pins (1 cm, fine gauge) and wood glue.
A hammer or pin punch.
The work
Step 1: Mark and cut all pieces

Use the combination square to mark all cut lines square across the board. Mark the knife line on the waste side of each pencil line, the tenon saw cuts on the waste side of the knife line. Cut all six pieces and label them. Check each piece is square end-to-end with the square.
Step 2: Dry fit before gluing

Assemble the tray without glue to check the fit. The long sides fit along the long edges of the base; the short sides butt against the end grain of the long sides. The divider sits between the long sides at one-third of the length. Check that the assembly sits square and flat before applying glue.
Step 3: Glue and pin

Apply wood glue to each joint surface. Assemble in order: long sides to base first, then short sides, then divider. Drive two panel pins through each joint. Check the assembly is square by measuring the diagonals, equal diagonals mean a square assembly. Clamp or weight the assembly while the glue sets (30 minutes for most PVA wood glues).
Step 4: Sand

After the glue is set, sand the outside surfaces with 120 grit, then 240 grit. Ease the top corners with a light sanding pass to remove the sharp arrises. No finish is necessary for a desk pencil tray, leave as natural pine, or apply a wax finish for a slight sheen.

attrs.symptom: The tray assembly is not square, one corner is at an angle
attrs.cause: One of the pieces was not cut square, or the assembly shifted before the glue set
attrs.fix: Before the glue sets: tap the long corner gently with a mallet to correct. After the glue sets: the joint cannot be re-squared, use this as a learning experience and remake the one non-square piece.
